Q: Swift decoding error on date type based on user settings preferences (time format) A:

DateFormatter respects the user’s locale and time-format settings by default.

Because of that, date decoding can fail on devices with different regional or 12/24-hour preferences, even when the backend response itself is correct.

To make date decoding predictable and independent of system settings, it’s recommended to use a fixed formatter, such as a DateFormatter configured with en_US_POSIX, or ISO8601DateFormatter.

Apple documentation explicitly recommends this approach for parsing fixed-format dates.

Using DateFormatter - Apple Documentation - DateFromatter

let formatter = DateFormatter()
formatter.locale = Locale(identifier: "en_US_POSIX")
formatter.timeZone = TimeZone(secondsFromGMT: 0)
formatter.dateFormat = "yyyy-MM-dd'T'HH:mm:ssZ"

Using ISO8601DateFormatter - Apple Documentation - iso8601dateformatter
Create manually in your context

let isoFormatter = ISO8601DateFormatter()
isoFormatter.formatOptions = [
    .withInternetDateTime,
    .withFractionalSeconds
]

Integrating with JSONDecoder

let jsonDecoder = JSONDecoder()

jsonDecoder.dateDecodingStrategy = .formatted(formatter) // en_US_POSIX
// or
jsonDecoder.dateDecodingStrategy = .custom { decoder in // ISO8601DateFormatter
    let container = try decoder.singleValueContainer()
    let dateString = try container.decode(String.self)

    let isoFormatter = ISO8601DateFormatter()
    isoFormatter.formatOptions = [
        .withInternetDateTime,
        .withFractionalSeconds
    ]

    guard let date = isoFormatter.date(from: dateString) else {
        throw DecodingError.dataCorruptedError(
            in: container,
            debugDescription: "Invalid ISO 8601 date: \(dateString)"
        )
    }

    return date
}

Recommended approach:
• At app boundaries (network / persistence) - Decode dates using ISO8601DateFormatter or a fixed DateFormatter
• Inside the app - Work only with Date
• In the UI layer - Format dates using locale-aware formatters (Locale.current)

This keeps your decoding logic stable while still respecting the user’s locale when displaying dates.

Q: How can I make WordPress handle .php URLs instead of returning a 404 error? A:

By default, WordPress only routes WordPress URLs (posts, pages, CPTs) through the core routing system and blocks direct access to custom .php files for security and rewrite consistency. you can try any one of them.

1. Put the .php Outside WordPress Routing

If you want a .php file to be accessed directly, place it above the WordPress root or outside of the routing rules.

Example:

/public_html/myfile.php

Then access:

https://example.com/myfile.php

2. Allow .php Access with Rewrite Rules

Update your .htaccess before the WordPress block:

# Allow direct PHP files
RewriteRule ^(.+)\.php$ $1.php [L]

Make sure this is before the WordPress rule:

# BEGIN WordPress
RewriteEngine On
RewriteBase /
...

This ensures Apache serves .php directly before WordPress tries to interpret it.

3. Serve via a WordPress Template (Safer)

Instead of direct .php, create a custom page template:

In theme: template-test.php

<?php
/*
Template Name: Test PHP Handler
*/
echo "This is served by WordPress!";

Then create a page in admin and select this template.

Why This Happens

WordPress uses rewrite rules to redirect requests to index.php.
Requests for .php are often rejected unless explicitly allowed because WordPress handles URLs via its permalink system, not direct file loading.
Allowing direct .php access without proper routing often requires rearranging .htaccess or using custom template routing.

If the goal is to run dynamic code within WordPress context, don’t serve standalone .php files — use:

  • Custom page templates

  • Shortcodes

  • REST API endpoints

These methods integrate smoothly with the WordPress system and avoid rewrite conflicts.
